candidates.title: Transient contacts between filaments impart its elasticity to branched actin
candidates.authors: Mehdi Bouzid, Cesar Valencia-Gallardo, Magdalena Kopec, Lara Koehler, Giuseppe Foffi, Olivia du Roure, Julien Heuvingh, Martin Lenz
candidates.abstract: Cells dynamically assemble actin into branched networks to push on their environment during cell migration, endocytosis or the maintenance of cell–cell contact1. These networks are among the stiffest found in the cytoskeleton and can generate large pushing stresses against stationary obstacles2–5. When grown against a controlled opposing stress in an atomic force microscope6 or inside the cell7, branched networks alter their own architecture to adapt their compressional stiffness to their environment, but the underpinnings of their mechanics and adaptability are unclear. Here we show that their high density and low connectivity place them outside the scope of standard elastic network models for actin. We show that they are instead dominated by the proliferation of interfilament contacts under compression. This places branched actin in the same category as undercoordinated fibrous materials such as sheep’s wool. When the network is grown under force, filaments entangle as if knitted together and trap contacts in their structure. Trapped contacts have a similar role as crosslinkers in rigidifying the network and are thus key to its active adaptive mechanics. Stiffness of branched actin networks emerges from the formation of contacts between filaments, with growth under load resulting in stiffer networks.

candidates.authors: Z. Wang, C. Moulsdale, X. Guo, J. Liu, Z. Qiu, I. Soltero, Z. Jiang, M. Holwill, J. Wu, H. Sun, Z. Chai, A. J. H. Jones, M. Zhu, J. Yin, C. P. Y. Wong, T. Taniguchi, K. candidates.abstract: Abstract van der Waals heterostructures are stabilized by a delicate balance between van der Waals, elastic and Coulomb energies 1–4 . Because the interfaces are not covalently bonded, the constituent crystals can slide, rotate and reconstruct, resulting in several possible competing structural phases 2,5,6 . However, controlled tuning of this balance, and hence dynamical control over the stacking, has yet to be achieved. Here we report a dynamical heterostructure in which monolayer graphene is doubly aligned to bulk hexagonal boron nitride (hBN) and monolayer hexagonal boron nitride (mhBN) on either side. In such a system, a global structural phase transition, manifested as a change of crystalline symmetry observed by scanning tunnelling microscopy, could be induced by gating, magnetic field or temperature. This structural transition is accompanied by an exotic electronic transition: the doping of graphene switches between discrete levels, corresponding to an exact integer number of electrons or holes per moiré plaquette. We attribute this integer doping to charge trapping in localized, strain-induced pseudo-Landau levels (flat bands in reciprocal space 7–12 ), produced by moiré reconstruction (strongly enhanced by the mhBN). Electrical control of coupled structural and electronic phase transitions provides a route to engineering strain-induced flat bands and strain–Coulomb correlations in van der Waals heterostructures.

candidates.abstract: Current understanding of the host tissue response to solid tumours is largely based on investigations of tumour types in isolation1. Given the breadth and diversity of human tumour pathology and contributions of tumour microenvironment (TME) cells to disease progression, pan-cancer analysis is needed to bridge major themes of stromal and immune cell evolution. To date, however, efforts to compare the TME response across cancers have been limited in scope2,3. Here we conduct a comprehensive pan-cancer analysis by algorithmically screening thousands of publicly available single-cell transcriptomic datasets for stromal and immune signatures across species and tissue types. We demonstrate conserved hallmarks of host cell transcriptional programming in response to malignancy across 42 cancer types in more than 2,000 human and mouse tumour samples. These findings are codified as an interactive web atlas ( tmeatlas.stanford.edu ) and software package (scTME) that will serve as practical resources for the systematic interrogation of the TME in tumours. A pan-cancer single-cell analysis of the tumour microenvironment across 42 cancer types and across 2 species is described.

candidates.title: Closest relatives of poxviruses prevail in human and animal guts worldwide
candidates.authors: Morgan Gaïa, Ulysse Guyet, Hans-Joachim Ruscheweyh, A. Murat Eren, Shinichi Sunagawa, Eugene V. Koonin, Mart Krupovic, Tom O. Delmont
candidates.abstract: Abstract Large and giant double-stranded DNA viruses substantially affect eukaryotic ecology and evolution 1–4 . They prevail in the environment but are rarely found in the digestive system of animals 5,6 . Here we present the discovery of a diversified group of DNA viruses with large linear genomes, dubbed egoviruses, that comprise a putative viral order most closely related to animal-infecting poxviruses. Egoviruses are found worldwide, almost exclusively in the digestive system of humans, livestock and wild animals. The most prevalent human-specific egovirus is spread across continents, demonstrating a long-term association between egoviruses and the human gut microbiome. Eukaryotic homologues of egovirus core genes suggest that these viruses primarily infect Trichostomatia (ciliates), which assist ruminant digestive processes 7 , and Parabasalia (Metamonada), which influence animal immunity and gut microbiome ecology 8 . Egoviruses also contributed to the genetic makeup of polintons, endogenous viruses that proliferated in genomes of Trichomonas vaginalis 9 and its close Parabasalia relatives. Unlike poxviruses that form brick-shaped virions, egoviruses are predicted to form multilayered icosahedral capsids resembling those of asfuviruses and probably representing the ancestral virion structure. Egoviruses are the only known clade of double-stranded DNA viruses of eukaryotes prevailing in the animal digestive system. Phylogenomic analysis suggests an evolutionary scenario whereby egovirus-like ancestors of poxviruses infected anaerobic unicellular eukaryotes inside the gut of ancestral animals, before transitioning to animal cell infection, which was accompanied by the virion metamorphosis.

candidates.title: Injury-induced signalling coordinates immunity and cannibalism in locusts
candidates.authors: Weikang Han, Tingting Lu, Wenkun Xie, Jinxi Yuan, Chengwei Lu, Lei Shang, Guirong Wang, Bill S. Hansson, Hetan Chang
candidates.abstract: Abstract Cannibalism, the consumption of conspecifics, is widespread across the animal kingdom and can profoundly influence individual fitness and population dynamics 1,2 . Although the ecological and social conditions that favour cannibalism have been well documented 2 , the molecular signals that trigger cannibalistic attacks have remained poorly understood. Here we show that in Locusta migratoria , guaiacol, a volatile compound with augmented release after injury, attracts gregarious nymphs and induces cannibalistic behaviour. Guaiacol is detected by olfactory receptors LmOR36 and LmOR34, and disruption of either receptor abolishes attraction, thereby impairing induction of cannibalism. Guaiacol is synthesized by haemolymph symbiont Enterobacter hormaechei . Injury promotes bacterial congregation at the wound site, leading to elevated guaiacol production through a clustered set of vanillic acid decarboxylase genes; deletion of this gene cluster abolishes guaiacol production and its behavioural effects. Notably, guaiacol initially functions as a beneficial signal after injury. Guaiacol activates immune-related pathways in wounded locusts, enhancing pathogen resistance and increasing survival following minor injury. However, when guaiacol emission exceeds a threshold determined by injury severity, it functions as an external cue that attracts cannibals. Cannibalistic locusts exploit this immune-related odour to locate severely injured conspecifics, gaining both nutritional resources and immune system benefits. Together, our findings identify a microbial–chemical mechanism that links immune defence with cannibalistic behaviour and provide potential molecular targets for manipulation of cannibalism-dependent population dynamics.

candidates.title: Hypothalamic volume and cell-type changes in ageing and Alzheimer’s disease
candidates.authors: Doudou Yu, Jürgen Germann, Ghulam Murtaza, Kaitlyn H. Hajdarovic, Kelsey R. Babcock, Shiva Kazempour Dehkordi, Alexander C. Jackson, Ivana Delalle, Miranda E. Orr, Habil Zare, Ritambhara Singh, Michael J. MacCoss, William Stafford Noble, Andrei G. Vlassenko, Manu S. Goyal, Ashley E. Webb
candidates.abstract: Alterations in metabolism, stress response, sleep, circadian rhythms and neuroendocrine processes are key features of ageing and neurodegeneration1,2. These fundamental processes are regulated by the hypothalamus, yet how its functionally distinct subregions and cell types change during human ageing and Alzheimer’s disease (AD) remains largely unexplored. Here we present HypoAD, an atlas of the human hypothalamus in ageing and AD, including high-resolution magnetic resonance imaging from 458 individuals and single-nucleus RNA sequencing of 614,403 nuclei from young participants, patients with AD and age-matched non-dementia control participants. We show that hypothalamic subregions governing metabolism, stress and circadian rhythms are particularly vulnerable, showing notable changes in both volumes and gene expression during ageing and AD. At the molecular level, machine learning models identified the inflammatory response and regulators of circadian rhythms as key cellular predictors of AD. These signatures were reflected in specific cell types: microglia transitioned to a pro-inflammatory state, whereas inhibitory neurons within sleep-regulating and circadian-regulating hypothalamic subregions showed the most profound transcriptional alterations, including disruptions in ligand–receptor interactions and G-protein-coupled receptor signalling. HypoAD provides a high-resolution volumetric map and a transcriptomic atlas of the human hypothalamus in ageing and AD, relating lifestyle and behavioural changes to the relevant volumetric and molecular pathways. In addition, HypoAD provides a framework to investigate hypothalamic dysfunction and establishes a roadmap for targeted interventions aimed at mitigating physiological disruptions to potentially slow disease progression. candidates.title: Global patterns and drivers of bee richness and endemism on islands
candidates.authors: Leon Marshall, John S. Ascher, Robert J. Whittaker, Michael C. Orr, Alice C. Hughes, Julian Schrader, Patrick Weigelt, Holger Kreft, Nicolas J. Vereecken
candidates.abstract: Islands account for a disproportionate share of global biodiversity1, yet insects, including invaluable pollinators such as bees2, remain underrepresented in island biogeography research3. Here we present a global checklist of island bees, recording 4,147 species across 305 islands. Although islands comprise only about 6% of the Earth’s land area, they support around 20% of known global bee diversity, and 42% of insular species are endemic, making up around 8% of all known bee species. Island bee species richness peaks at mid-latitudes (at least in the Northern Hemisphere), mirroring continental trends4. Native richness increases with island area and declines with isolation, consistent with patterns in other taxa5. The strength of island species–area relationships varies among biomes and is steepest in Mediterranean-type systems, which also support disproportionately high bee richness relative to flowering plant diversity. The number of endemic species is highest on large tropical islands, reflecting extensive in situ diversification. Major centres of bee endemism include Madagascar, Malesia (the Greater Sundas and New Guinea) and the Hawaiian islands, where a single large radiation of Hylaeus (Nesoprosopis) dominates6. Among islands that are capable of supporting endemic species, endemism scales strongly with total richness. These findings highlight the need to integrate island bee diversity into global conservation planning and position bees as a model for understanding insect evolution and conservation on islands. Gobal analysis of bee species across 305 islands reveals that islands account for 20% of global bee diversity, with more than 4,100 species and high levels of endemism, and shows that richness is shaped by island size, isolation and evolutionary diversification.

candidates.abstract: Abstract Photonic integrated circuits are emerging as a key technology for compact, analogue and energy-efficient optical information processing 1 . Yet, their practical implementation remains limited by the intrinsically weak optical nonlinearities of conventional materials, which demand high power and large device footprints to achieve substantial nonlinear responses 2 . Exciton–polaritons, hybrid light–matter excitations of semiconducting materials, offer a promising route to overcome these limitations by combining strong optical nonlinearities with the high speed and scalability typical of photonic platforms 3–5 . However, despite their potential, fully integrated on-chip polaritonic systems simultaneously delivering room-temperature waveguide lasing, controllable optical routing and amplification have remained elusive. Here we demonstrate a fully integrated perovskite polaritonic circuit that brings these functionalities together in a single-step-grown platform. We realize precise and scalable polariton circuits with integrated gratings that act as both couplers and reflectors, enabling in-plane Fabry–Pérot cavities. These structures support robust in-plane polariton lasing with coherent guided emission at a geometry-defined wavelength, optical amplification of propagating polaritons and nonlinear optical phase control exceeding π, all within the same on-chip architecture. Our results establish perovskite polariton circuits as a scalable platform for active and interferometric integrated photonics.

candidates.title: Observation of tunable superradiant frequency combs
candidates.authors: Tian Xie, Rikuto Fukumori, Wai-Keong Mok, Jiahui Li, Joonhee Choi, Andrei Faraon
candidates.abstract: Cavity quantum electrodynamics1 with quantum emitters coupled to resonators provides a powerful platform for engineering light–matter interactions2,3 and exploring many-body phenomena4,5. In particular, superradiance6—arising from collective quantum interference among emitters—has been explored as a route to ultrastable continuous radiation7. However, engineering superradiance in the time domain to realize periodic pulsed sources or frequency combs remains largely unexplored. Here we investigate the non-equilibrium many-body dynamics of a driven spin ensemble coupled with an on-chip superconducting resonator and uncover a dynamical phase transition from continuous-wave to periodic pulsed superradiant emission. To quantitatively capture the observed dynamical phases, we introduce a driven-dissipative cavity-quantum electrodynamics model that elucidates how the periodic pulsed superradiant phase emerges from collective, periodically repeating spin dynamics stabilized by the interplay of coherence growth, disorder and dissipation. We also find that rare-earth ion spin systems with both optical and microwave transitions enable phase-synchronized, dual-rail superradiant frequency combs in both the microwave and the optical domains. Our results not only open new opportunities for atom-based frequency-comb sources and programmable superradiant generation, but establish a fundamental connection between periodic pulsed superradiance and the emergence of a continuous time crystal8–10 as a new non-equilibrium phase in driven open systems. A transition from continuous to periodic pulsed superradiant emission in coupled spin–resonator systems is demonstrated, revealing connections to time crystals and enabling synchronized microwave and optical frequency combs.

candidates.abstract: Abstract Ferroptosis, a form of cell death induced by overwhelming membrane lipid peroxidation, is a vulnerability of many cancers, including cancers resistant to current molecular and immune-based therapies 1–7 . Triggering of ferroptosis therefore provides an opportunity to achieve elimination of difficult-to-treat cancers 1–4,8,9 . Studies in mouse cancer models have demonstrated that anticancer immunity, mediated by dendritic cells (DCs) and CD8 + T cells, is essential for effective tumour eradication by ferroptosis-inducing strategies 10–13 . However, ferroptotic cells limit this response 8–10,14 , resulting in immune escape and tumour growth through mechanisms that remain unclear. Here we demonstrate that ferroptotic cancer cells activate a molecular program resulting in aberrant production of prostaglandin E 2 (PGE 2 ), which limits the stimulation of anticancer CD8 + T cell responses by type 1 conventional DCs (cDC1s), thereby promoting immune escape. In ferroptotic cancer cells, lipid peroxidation-mediated membrane permeabilization enables Ca 2+ influx, which activates p38 MAPK signalling and thereby drives PGE 2 production. This signalling axis is uncoupled from cancer cell death and can be targeted to selectively interfere with immune-inhibitory PGE 2 production while preserving ferroptotic cancer cell elimination. In the context of cancer cell ferroptosis, ablation of PGE 2 production or disrupting PGE 2 signalling restores cDC1-mediated anticancer CD8 + T cell responses and leads to effective tumour elimination. Our findings identify a key mechanism that limits antitumour immunity and prevents tumour elimination upon ferroptosis induction in cancer cells, which could be exploited for cancer therapy.

candidates.authors: Weijun Xiu, Qian Wang, Ling Wan, Zhuoming Liang, Michael Raphael Panganiban, Xiaoye Li, Ao He, Yu Zhang, Heng Dong, Yu Fu, Lianhui Wang, Yuxin Liu
candidates.abstract: Metabolic disorders such as diabetes mellitus are global health crises driven by metabolic imbalance, chronic inflammation and dysfunction of the neuroimmune axis1–3. Electroceuticals targeting the autonomic nervous system have shown anti-inflammatory effects, yet existing systems lack the metabolic interoceptive feedback to fully restore immune–metabolic homeostasis4–9. Analogous to its biological counterpart, NeuroAxis is solely powered by endogenous glucose, operating without batteries or wireless power transfer. In both models, NeuroAxis restores glucose tolerance, improves insulin sensitivity and normalizes glycaemic control, with therapeutic effects persisting after treatment cessation. Our artificial neuroimmune axis promotes substantial advances in treating metabolic disorders and represents a general approach for autonomously regulating interorgan communication, central to homeostasis and pathophysiology. candidates.abstract: A major goal in neuroscience is to map the transformation of information as it flows through the brain. For example, neurons at many levels of the visual hierarchy are attuned to motion direction1–5. However, links between motion-selective computations and cell types at various stages of the visual hierarchy remain unidentified. A key first step in delineating these relationships is to map the wiring diagrams that connect different motion-selective cell types. Here we establish a systematic, cell-type-specific circuit-mapping method, combining an anterograde trans-neuronal fluorescent tracer (mWGA–mCherry)6 with spatial transcriptomics (multiplexed error-robust fluorescence in situ hybridization (MERFISH))7,8 to establish TransA-MERFISH. These experiments unexpectedly revealed that retinal on–off direction-selective ganglion cells (ooDSGCs) innervate several direction-selective SC cell types, but do not innervate a SC cell type that was previously reported to display strong direction-selective responses. We validated these results using orthogonal approaches and demonstrated the sensitivity and specificity of TransA-MERFISH. Functional studies of SC activity before and after ablation of retinal direction-selective circuits confirmed that these computationally distinct, ooDSGC-dependent and -independent direction-selective cell types are commingled in SC. Together, our study establishes TransA-MERFISH as a robust framework for mapping wiring diagrams at the cell-type level and uncovers divergent computational mechanisms of motion detection in early visual processing. Here we provide an ecosystem-wide assessment of 24 taxonomic groups across all domains of life—encompassing 40,049 species—along a land-use intensification gradient from lowland forests to intensively managed smallholder cash-crop monocultures in Indonesian landscapes. Despite widespread losses of landscape and local multidiversity 1 in monocultures (approximately 78% and 50%, respectively), we found no evidence for consistent community homogenization with land-use intensification. Instead, monocultures exhibit a systematic shift from turnover to nestedness for aboveground taxa. Such patterns of differentiation may mask trajectories towards biotic homogenization via early stages of assemblage simplification. Biotic differentiation has the potential to partly mitigate biodiversity losses by positively affecting γ-diversity. This opens management options, including the conservation of existing remnants of traditional agriculture and the implementation of sustainable management practices 2–4 . Our results demonstrate that tropical land-use intensification restructures biodiversity not only through species loss, but also via a pervasive reorganization of community composition across trophic levels. Conserving tropical biodiversity, therefore, requires a multi-taxon, landscape-scale perspective that explicitly integrates agricultural land uses with the protection of natural and semi-natural habitats to reconcile agricultural production and conservation.

candidates.authors: Simon Wili, Meng-Zi Huang, Tommaso Bonaccorsi, Michael U. Mühlematter, Mohsen Talebi, Yaakov Yudkin, Alex Gómez-Salvador, Filip Marijanovic, Eugene Demler, Tilman Esslinger
candidates.abstract: Abstract Resistance in standard conductors decreases with increasing cross-section. Yet, in low-dimensional superconductors and superfluids, residual resistance arises from topological fluctuations of the order parameter, manifesting as phase slips in one-dimensional (1D) and vortices in two-dimensional (2D) systems. How resistance and dissipation evolve as geometry interpolates between these regimes remains an open question. This evolution is masked in solid-state experiments by disorder, impurities and geometric imperfections 1–3 , and poses theoretical challenges due to competing dissipative processes and pronounced finite-size effects. Here, we use a defect-free unitary Fermi gas in a digitally programmable transport geometry to isolate geometric effects on superfluid dissipation and discover a paradox: in the crossover from one dimension to two dimensions, the resistance reaches a minimum. There, widening a channel increases its resistance. Narrower, quasi-1D channels show dissipation described by Langer–Ambegaokar–McCumber–Halperin theory of phase slips 4 . In this regime, varying the channel width yields the predicted exponential scaling of the activation factor over many orders of magnitude. Wider, quasi-2D channels show dissipation consistent with phase-slip events described by a finite-size vortex model 5 . The minimal dissipation in the dimensional crossover reflects a transition in the dominant dissipative mechanism, with both 1D and 2D events simultaneously suppressed. Our measurements suggest a route to minimizing dissipation in superconducting devices and provide a benchmark for theoretical efforts aimed at describing the dimensional crossover.

candidates.abstract: Abstract The genus Hordeum comprises cultivated barley and its wild relatives, an evolutionarily, ecologically and agriculturally important group of grasses 1,2 . Here we generated a chromosome-scale comparative genomic resource comprising all recognized diploid Hordeum species together with representative polyploid lineages. Comparative analyses reveal extensive structural variation, including inversions and chromosomal rearrangements that disrupt proximal collinearity and reflect lineage-specific genome remodelling. Single-copy gene phylogenies identify ancient hybridization, segmental exchange and introgression, revealing pervasive reticulate evolution during Hordeum diversification. We uncover widespread horizontal gene transfer from Panicoideae grasses into Hordeum , with many transferred genes showing evidence of transcription and functional integration. Retrotransposon proliferation explains genome size variation and provides insights into polyploid genome evolution. Whole-genome alignments reveal contrasting evolutionary dynamics: whereas coding sequences remain highly conserved, regulatory elements undergo rapid turnover, providing a rich source of regulatory diversity for phenotypic evolution. Case studies of vernalization and glume development demonstrate how natural variation in regulatory and coding sequences contributes to flowering time and floral morphology. This comprehensive pangenomic framework establishes Hordeum as a model for studying genome evolution, structural variation and the genetic basis of adaptive traits, offering new avenues for barley improvement.

candidates.title: Quantum position verification with remote untrusted devices
candidates.authors: Gautam A. Kavuri, Yanbao Zhang, Abigail R. Gookin, Soumyadip Patra, Joshua C. Bienfang, Honghao Fu, Yusuf Alnawakhtha, Dileep V. Reddy, Michael D. Mazurek, Carlos Abellán, Waldimar Amaya, Morgan W. Mitchell, Carl A. Miller, Richard P. Mirin, Martin J. Stevens, Scott Glancy, Emanuel Knill, Lynden K. Shalm
candidates.abstract: Position information underpins many modern technologies, from navigation and timing to authentication and critical infrastructure1–3. However, classical methods of proving that information originates from a particular position are vulnerable to spoofing4–6. This limitation can be overcome with quantum technologies7–16, but current protocols rely on trust in quantum hardware that can be undermined17,18, or require quantum computers and bounds on adversarial computation19. Nevertheless, there has been considerable interest in experimental demonstrations, and aspects of these protocols have been implemented20–22. Here we introduce and experimentally demonstrate the Bell-test quantum position verification protocol for device-independent quantum position verification that guarantees security with only observed correlations from a loophole-free Bell test23–25 across a quantum network. In the experiment, we implement a version of this device-independent protocol against adversaries who, before each trial, are weakly entangled. Our demonstration achieves a one-dimensional localization 2.47(2) times smaller than the best, necessarily non-remote, classical localization protocol. Compared with classical protocols with identical latencies, the localization volume is 4.53(5) times smaller, representing a certifiable quantum advantage. The general Bell-test protocol is loss-tolerant and secure against adversaries with substantial quantum resources. This work allows digital security to be anchored to physically trusted locations, enabling new position-based authentication protocols for applications such as financial transactions, legal agreements and securing critical infrastructure26–29. A loophole-free Bell-test quantum protocol demonstrates secure, device-independent position verification, achieving up to 4.53-fold smaller localization volumes than classical methods and enabling tamper-resistant location-based authentication.

candidates.title: Evidence for p-wave magnetism in electronic band structure of metallic EuSi
candidates.authors: Erjian Cheng, Yixing Yang, Yifan Gao, Jan Priessnitz, Yiqing Hao, Jieyi Liu, Rui Lou, Alexander Fedorov, Mengyu Yao, Yuri Prots, Houke Chen, Ralf Koban, Xuemin Shi, Ying-Ting Chan, Ulrich Burkhardt, Berit H. candidates.abstract: Abstract One active frontier of quantum-matter research is the realization of p -wave symmetry-breaking phases in fermionic systems, long exemplified by the A phase of superfluid helium-3 (refs. 1–3 ). Achieving p -wave superconductivity 4 and its magnetic analogue 5 —characterized by a time-reversal-symmetric, p -wave spin-polarized Fermi surface—remains a grand challenge 6,7 . Despite recent progress in identifying candidate p -wave magnets 5,7–10 , spin-resolved spectroscopic evidence for their electronic structures remains limited. Here we report angle-resolved photoemission spectroscopy (ARPES) and spin-ARPES evidence for p -wave magnetism in the near-Fermi-level electronic structure of stoichiometric metallic EuSi, supported by symmetry analysis, first-principles calculations and neutron scattering. Neutron diffraction reveals a chiral spiral phase between 33.4 K and 62 K that fulfils archetypal p -wave magnetism criteria: it preserves the combined symmetry of time reversal and lattice translation, while breaking inversion symmetry. Spin-integrated ARPES reveals a pronounced magnetism-driven reconstruction of the electronic structure, with energy separations exceeding 100 meV, and spin-ARPES resolves S y polarization in near-Fermi-level spectral features. The extracted S y exhibits a sign-changing modulation across successive magnetic Brillouin zones and is suppressed near the nodal regions, consistent with the predicted p -wave spin texture and unfolded spin-polarization calculations. Magnetic force microscopy and micro-ARPES further reveal approximately 10-μm chiral magnetic domains. These results identify EuSi as a stoichiometric metallic platform for investigating p -wave magnetism in electronic band structures and spin-symmetry-based functionalities in spintronics 10 , topological matter 7 , superconductivity 11 and beyond.

candidates.title: Rainforest adaptation in late Homo erectus from southern China
candidates.authors: K. E. Westaway, R. Joannes-Boyau, W. Liao, Q. Shao, W. Yu, M. Quinn, A.-M. Bacon, H. Liang, N. Bourgon, J.-x. Zhao, P. Roberts, R. Kono, Y. Pan, L. Yang, Y. Wang, C. Jin, Z. candidates.abstract: Homo erectus represents one of the longest-persisting hominin species, with a geographic range from Africa to eastern Eurasia from approximately 1.9 million years ago1 to 108 thousand years ago (ka)2. Despite this, there are still large gaps in our understanding of the adaptation capabilities of this species and the extent of its persistence in China. Assumptions over ecological preferences based on the Trinil3, Sangiran4 and Ngandong2 (in Java) open woodland–grassland mosaics have persisted, combined with limited direct stable carbon isotope measurements in Asia. Here we present a rich temporal and environmental context for nine hominin teeth, eight of which were morphologically and genetically identified as H. erectus5, found in two sister caves in Guangxi province, southern China. We modelled 43 radiometric ages from five dating techniques to establish a timeline for H. erectus presence in this region. Stable and clumped isotopes and trace elements from teeth were used to establish the dominant environments and their behavioural responses. We show that H. erectus was present in southern China between 324 and 184 ka, which is substantially more recent than previously established in this region for unequivocally H. erectus fossils at approximately 400 ka. The evidence suggests that they were persisting in closed rainforest ecosystems, thought to be the domain of only Homo sapiens, and were demonstrating long-term mobility and ecological flexibility. This evidence challenges the assumptions over the ecological preferences and behavioural limitations of H. erectus. Eight Homo erectus teeth from two caves in southern China reveal that the species persisted in closed rainforest ecosystems between 324 and 184 ka, challenging assumptions about their ecological preferences and behavioural limitations.

candidates.title: Analogue simulation of massive relativistic quantum fields in 2 + 1 dimensions
candidates.authors: Yansheng Zhang, Feiyang Wang, Paul H. C. Wong, Alexander C. Jenkins, Yi Jiang, Konstantinos Konstantinou, Gehrig Carlse, Nishant Dogra, Joseph H. Thywissen, Christoph Eigen, Zoran Hadzibabic
candidates.abstract: Abstract Quantum field theories provide fundamental models of complex interacting systems 1–3 , from high-energy physics and cosmology to condensed matter. However, solving these models in non-perturbative and dynamical regimes is often challenging, particularly in more than one spatial dimension. Analogue simulation using tunable synthetic quantum systems can both verify existing theoretical predictions and lead to physical insights. Here we realize analogue simulation of massive relativistic quantum fields in 2 + 1 dimensions (two spatial dimensions and time), using two coherently coupled spin components 4,5 in a uniform two-dimensional atomic Bose–Einstein condensate 6,7 . Specifically, we encode the paradigmatic sine-Gordon model 8,9 in the long-wavelength modes of the field describing the relative phase, ϕ , of the two components. In the perturbative regime, collective field excitations exhibit a relativistic dispersion with a tunable mass gap. We also observe explicitly non-perturbative phenomena, including the existence of topological domain walls across which ϕ rapidly winds by 2π (ref. 10 ). Our work opens possibilities for studies of cosmologically relevant phenomena including preheating 11,12 , dynamics of topological defects 13,14 and relativistic false-vacuum decay 15–19 .

candidates.title: Widespread deciduousness reveals diverse Amazonian phenological strategies
candidates.authors: Guangqin Song, Alice C. Hughes, Xu Lian, Xiang Zeng, Scott R. Saleska, Alfredo Huete, Loren P. Albert, Xiangtao Xu, Josep Peñuelas, Constantin M. Zohner, Matteo Detto, S. candidates.abstract: The Amazon rainforest is a cornerstone of regional and global carbon cycling1 and is widely regarded and modelled as a perennially evergreen ecosystem2,3. This prevailing view, however, masks substantial fine-scale variation in leaf phenology, limiting our capacity to predict ecosystem responses to climate change. Here by combining 10-m Sentinel-2 observations with machine learning, we uncover pervasive, spatially structured seasonal deciduousness across the basin. In 70.0% of the Amazon, leaf shedding precedes leaf flushing by at least 3 months, creating pronounced asynchrony between deciduousness and greenness seasonality, whereas the remainder shows near-synchronous phenology. Hydroclimate emerges as the dominant factor associated with this asynchrony across 51.6% of the area, followed by soil properties (33.2%) and light availability (15.2%). Motivated by this widespread decoupling between deciduousness and canopy greenness, we incorporated deciduousness-constrained leaf turnover and the resulting leaf-age demography into ecophysiological models, yielding spatially widespread improvements in the seasonal agreement between simulated gross primary productivity and satellite-derived photosynthetic seasonality across 79.9% of the basin. These findings challenge the conventional view of Amazonian phenology, demonstrating that previously overlooked deciduousness influences Amazonian carbon dynamics. Incorporating these insights into process-based models is essential for refining projections of climate–forest feedbacks in the Amazon and for understanding its ecological functions under accelerating global change. A basin-wide assessment of Amazonian deciduousness using high-resolution satellite observations shows a diverse range of phenological strategies across the Amazon rainforest, contrary to the prevailing view of Amazonian phenology.

candidates.abstract: Hominin fossils and genetic evidence indicate that several hominin populations occupied East and Southeast Asia during the Middle and Late Pleistocene epoch1–10. Homo erectus fossils remain scarce in southern China and mainland Southeast Asia4,8,11. Here we report nine newly discovered late Middle Pleistocene hominin teeth from the Naxian and Baxian caves at the Chongzuo study area, Guangxi Zhuang Autonomous Region, southern China, dated to around 324–184 thousand years ago12. Palaeoproteomics reveals the presence of an endogenous dental proteome in all five hominin teeth studied molecularly. Four teeth contain a derived H. erectus substitution in ameloblastin that to date has been observed only in older Middle Pleistocene H. erectus specimens from China13. The proteomes of these four teeth differ from the previous H. erectus proteomes from China at another ameloblastin position, suggesting that these specimens represent a previously unsampled H. erectus population. Morphometric and geometric morphometric methods support an attribution of these teeth to H. erectus, as well as four additional teeth. This fills a gap in the geographical and chronological distribution of H. erectus in East Asia. The fifth tooth studied proteomically, PA1796, is morphologically distinct from H. erectus, Neanderthals (Homo neanderthalensis) and modern humans (Homo sapiens), and does not contain the H. erectus-derived amino acid sequence. The late survival of H. erectus on mainland East Asia suggests that at least two hominin lineages, H. erectus and Homo longi (Denisovans)6,7, possibly represented by PA1796, were present in the region towards the end of the Middle Pleistocene, with the first documented occurrence of H. sapiens not much later5. Late Middle Pleistocene hominin teeth from the Naxian and Baxian caves of southern China, dated to around 324–184 thousand years ago, fill a gap in the geographical and chronological distribution of Homo erectus in East Asia.

candidates.title: Bogong moths navigate with a light-dependent geomagnetic inclination compass
candidates.authors: Hui Chen, Linnea Rosberg, David Dreyer, Bo Leberecht, Henrik Mouritsen, Pauline N. Fleischmann, Eric J. Warrant
candidates.abstract: Abstract Bogong moths ( Agrotis infusa ) migrate biannually up to 1,000 km between their breeding areas and geographically restricted aestivation sites in the Australian Alps 1,2 . These moths navigate towards their distant goal using the stars as a compass 3 but navigate correctly even when the stars are obscured by clouds 3 , suggesting that their magnetic sense 4 probably harnesses the Earth’s magnetic field as a compass. However, the nature of this compass, and of the magnetic sense underlying it, remains unknown. Here we show that Bogong moths, tethered in a flight arena under a full-spectrum randomized starry night sky, navigate in their inherited migratory direction using the geomagnetic field alone. If the geomagnetic field is turned by 180°, or if inclination is inverted, moths fly in the opposite direction. If polarity is inverted, moths fail to turn. Furthermore, if violet–blue light (380 nm < λ < 500 nm) is removed from the illumination spectrum, or if tethered moths are exposed to weak broadband radiofrequency fields (150 kHz to 60 MHz), magnetic orientation is abolished. Our results indicate that Bogong moths use the geomagnetic field as an inclination compass for long-distance navigation at night and possess a light-dependent radical-pair-based magnetic sense 5 .

candidates.title: Band-Edge-Extended Heterointerfaces for Perovskite Solar Cells and Tandems
candidates.authors: Bitao Dong, Meijie Cui, Cong Chen, Ruoting Zhao, Huanxin Ju, Jingwei Xue, Yingguo Yang, Likai Zheng, Ling Zeng, Yanbiao Ran, Taixiang Li, Zhenyin Zhang, Gengsheng Chen, Jinggang Lan, Qunping Fan, Long Jiang, Shanglei Feng, Jiaxin Li, Wenyan Su, Yuxiang Li, Shaik Mohammed Zakeeruddin, Mingyang Wei, Wei Ma, Jie Kong, Michael Grätzel, Yuhang Liu
candidates.abstract: Perovskite solar cells (PSCs) have emerged as a promising photovoltaic technology, with efficiencies rapidly approaching those of established crystalline-silicon solar cells. Further efficiency gains, however, are increasingly limited by charge extraction and recombination at the interface between the perovskite absorber and the electron-transport layer. Interfacial modifiers are widely used to suppress these losses, yet many conventional ammonium-based modifiers are weakly electronically coupled to the perovskite surface and can introduce barriers to electron extraction 1-5. Here we realize electronically coupled heterointerfaces by introducing a family of heteroatom-containing, fully conjugated formamidinium interfacial modulators, establishing band-edge-extending conjugated heterointerfaces that overcome the bottleneck of inefficient interfacial electron transfer. The resulting band-edge-extended heterointerface establishes delocalized electron connectivity at the perovskite/electron transporting layer (ETL) interface and suppresses interfacial non-radiative recombination. We report a certified power-conversion efficiency (PCE) of 27.96% and a stabilized power output (SPO) of 27.84% for inverted PSCs. The corresponding devices retained over 95% of their initial efficiency after 2000 h continuous maximum-power-point tracking under 1-sun irradiation (ISOS-L). Extending this strategy to monolithic perovskite–silicon tandems enables a certified SPO of 34.71%, establishing band-edge extension as a broadly applicable approach to overcoming the conventional trade-off between interfacial passivation and charge extraction.

candidates.title: Designed broken symmetries facilitate configurational complexity in nematic vortex crystals
candidates.authors: Cuiling Meng, Žiga Kos, Jin-Sheng Wu, Cristiano Nisoli, Jörn Dunkel, Ivan I. Smalyukh
candidates.abstract: Abstract Although widely used in modern technological applications, liquid crystals have not yet been systematically explored or utilized as reconfigurable information storage devices. Here we demonstrate that precisely designed broken symmetries in nematic vortex crystal lattices give rise to exponential configurational complexity exceeding the configurational entropy of conventional atomic crystals, and arising from the manifold ways in which surface-anchored nematic defect lines can combine to form nematic vortex crystals with distinct free-energy minima and tailored broken symmetries, thereby generalizing the interstitial and substitutional defects as well as grain boundaries in conventional crystalline materials. We illustrate the versatility of our experimental platform by designing nematic vortex crystals with various broken symmetries and show how their topological states can be reconfigured on demand via laser-induced topological surgery. Thus, our results provide an experimental and conceptual foundation for the development of soft-matter-based topological memory and computation devices.

candidates.abstract: R-2-Hydroxyglutarate (R2HG), an oncometabolite predominantly produced by mutated isocitrate dehydrogenase 1/2 (IDH1/2) in various cancers, is known to drive cancer progression through noncovalent inhibition of α-ketoglutarate (αKG)-dependent enzymes. In this work, we propose an alternative mechanism wherein R2HG contributes to cancer development via covalent modification of biologically critical lysines, a process termed lysine-R2HGylation (KR2HG). We designed and synthesized R2HG-mimicking probes and demonstrated their effectiveness in facilitating KR2HG target profiling and site mapping. We identified KR2HG as a post-translational modification, confirmed its C5-linkage on GSTP1(K209), and demonstrated that SIRT5 functions as a deacylase for GSTP1-KR2HG in vitro. Furthermore, we found that R2HG slightly but significantly inhibits the enzymatic activity of GSTP1 through KR2HG and dramatically suppresses monocyte differentiation via this catalytically important lysine modification. Our findings provide an alternative perspective on the role of R2HG in leukemia progression and offer a practical tool for the clinical investigation of R2HG-elevated cancers. R-2-hydroxyglutarate is a cancer-linked metabolite whose mechanisms are incompletely understood. Here, the authors identify and structurally characterize lysineR2HGylation as a protein modification and develop probes that reveal GSTP1 as a functional target in leukemia cells.

candidates.title: An ingestible, bio-inspired self-powered electrocapsule for in situ ethanol clearance mitigates systemic and neurobehavioral toxicity
candidates.authors: Yiran Pu, Wenqi Wei, Yuanmeng He, Kai Yong, Mei Chen, Yajing Zhang, Yue Wu, Jiaxin Long, Yunxiang He, Gonghua Hong, Hao Wu, Junling Guo
candidates.abstract: Alcohol intoxication remains a pervasive driver of global mortality and multi-organ pathology, yet its clinical management is fundamentally limited by the saturation kinetics of hepatic enzymes and the rapid gastrointestinal absorption of ethanol. While ingestible bioelectronics have advanced physiological monitoring and neural modulation, autonomous systems that locally convert metabolically relevant toxins upon contact within the gastrointestinal tract remain underdeveloped. Here, we report a fully integrated, ingestible, and self-powered electrocapsule designed for localized intestinal ethanol interception. The device features a galvanic architecture utilizing biomimetically assembled manganese–ellagic acid (Mn–EA) mesocrystals. The device integrates a Zn-based galvanic component for self-powered operation with a Mn–EA/Au interface for contact-dependent ethanol conversion toward acetate, providing a host-independent auxiliary clearance pathway. In a rat model of acute intoxication, prophylactic administration reduced blood ethanol concentrations by ~58–68% across the 0.5–6 h observation window, shortened the duration of righting-reflex loss, and mitigated alcohol-induced neurobehavioral deficits and hepatic injury. This reduction in systemic ethanol exposure was achieved with minimal electrochemical interference from a representative biomolecule mixture in vitro. This work establishes a preclinical metabolic-bioelectronics platform for localized intestinal ethanol interception and motivates future scale-adjusted pharmacokinetic, gastrointestinal transit, and safety evaluations. Alcohol intoxication remains a leading cause of death and accidents. Here, the authors develop a self-powered electrocapsule that enables local intestinal ethanol conversion, reducing systemic ethanol exposure and associated toxicity in rats.

candidates.title: A revised genome annotation of the model cyanobacterium Synechocystis based on start and stop codon-enriched ribosome profiling and proteogenomics
candidates.authors: Lydia Hadjeras, Vanessa Krauspe, Rick Gelhausen, Benjamin Heiniger, Philipp Spät, Viktoria Reimann, Garance Jaques, Paul Minges, Raphael Bilger, Maren Gerstner, Boris Maček, Christian H. Ahrens, Rolf Backofen, Cynthia M. Sharma, Wolfgang R. Hess
candidates.abstract: Abstract Cyanobacteria are important primary producers and popular in biotechnology. Synechocystis 6803 is a model cyanobacterium, yet many coding regions are ambiguous, or have remained undetected. Here, we present a riboproteogenomic analysis combining ribosome profiling with inhibitors that stall ribosomes at translation initiation and termination sites, and proteogenomic re-annotation of its genome. Based on proteogenomics, we report translation of 3055 annotated genes (83%), 3492 based on Ribo-seq (95.2%), and 3,018 supported by both methods (82%). The data suggest additional protein-coding genes and corrections for annotated ones. We validate 15 proteins translated from antisense, intergenic and intragenic loci and provide proteogenomic support for up to 69 additional, mostly small proteins. We identify three genes with ~300 nt long intragenic out-of-frame translons and demonstrate that internal and host translons are translated into interacting proteins. Our data are accessible at https://www.bioinf.uni-freiburg.de/~ribobase/ . They illustrate the enormous value of consolidating genome annotations with integrated experimental data.

candidates.abstract: A comprehensive understanding of the Ras self-inactivation mechanism at atomic resolution—specifically, intrinsic GTP hydrolysis converting the GTP-bound active form to the GDP-bound inactive form—is essential for designing therapies against Ras-driven cancers. Conventional models describe a biphasic GTP-bound state: Ras interconverts between inactive state 1 and active, catalytically competent state 2. However, the structural pathway leading to Ras/GDP via these states remains unclear. Here, we use time-resolved serial femtosecond and synchrotron crystallography to capture GTP hydrolysis in Ras crystals loaded with photoactivatable caged GTP, across timescales from milliseconds to hours. Photolysis yielded Ras in state 1—a conformation lacking a stabilized nucleophilic water characteristic of state 2. Remarkably, this state persists for hours and converts directly to Ras/GDP without passing through state 2. These findings challenge the prevailing view that state 2 is essential and suggest that state 1 can directly support catalysis, offering an alternative conceptual basis for targeting clinically relevant Ras mutants that preferentially adopt this conformation. Ras proteins switch off by hydrolyzing GTP, but the structural pathway remains unclear. Here, authors use time-resolved crystallography to show that Ras can convert from state 1 directly to GDP without adopting state 2.

candidates.abstract: Aneuploidy and chromosomal instability are common characteristics of cancer but remain underexploited therapeutically. Chromosomally unstable cells are often selectively vulnerable to inhibition of the kinesin KIF18A, and this dependence is related to altered mitotic control. Here, we identify the spindle and kinetochore-associated (SKA) complex as a mitotic regulator that establishes a similar dependency. SKA complex loss is tolerated in cells with a defective mitotic checkpoint, but when mitosis is prolonged, it leads to mitotic errors and loss of viability. SKA complex depletion selectively impacts chromosomally unstable cancer cells and mirrors the effects of KIF18A inhibition. We thus identify a cellular vulnerability associated with prolonged mitosis in chromosomally unstable cancers. Targeting chromosome segregation in chromosomally unstable cancer cells holds promise for anti-cancer therapy. Here, Schoot Uiterkamp et al. identify the mitotic SKA complex as a potential target to combat chromosomally aberrant cancer.

candidates.authors: Xin Ge, Dingpu Liu, Haoran Wang, Yuhui Dong, Lin Li, Yifan Duan, Puxiu Shen, Yue Li, Jiaming Zhang, Yicheng Sun, Hairong Huang, Xiangmei Zhou, Ruichao Yue
candidates.abstract: Mycobacteria survive inside the immune cells meant to destroy them. Toxin-antitoxin systems, gene pairs that help bacteria withstand stress, are abundant in the Mycobacterium tuberculosis complex, yet their role in infection remains unclear. Here we show that the Mycobacterium bovis toxin VapC40 disrupts host nitrogen metabolism. VapC40 redirects glutamine catabolism in infected macrophages, producing excess glutamate and ammonia. Ammonia is transported into lysosomes through the transporter RHCG, raising their pH and rupturing their membranes. Ammonia then enters mitochondria, collapsing membrane potential and triggering oxidative damage. VapC40 recruits NIX to the damaged mitochondria and activates TBK1 on their surface, inducing mitophagy. At the same time, autophagosome maturation is impaired and fewer bacteria reach lysosomes, so the pathogen escapes clearance. Mice infected with VapC40-deficient bacteria show less ammonia toxicity and lung necrosis. These findings show that mycobacteria manipulate host nitrogen metabolism, and identify ammonia-induced organelle damage as a potential therapeutic target. In this work, the authors show that a bacterial virulence factor from Mycobacterium bovis rewires nitrogen metabolism in infected immune cells, producing ammonia that damages lysosomes and mitochondria and allows the bacteria to avoid destruction.

candidates.title: Superionicity and premelting of iron-rich (Fe,Mg)O at Earth’s core-mantle boundary
candidates.authors: Wei Zhang, Tao Wang, Guilin Liu, Zhongfa Zhou, Duck Young Kim, Yu He
candidates.abstract: Abstract Core-mantle interactions are essential for understanding Earth’s interior dynamics and evolution. Experimental studies reveal that core-mantle reactions produce iron-rich (Fe,Mg)O (periclase‑wüstite solid solution). Here we show that Fe-rich (Fe,Mg)O exhibits pronounced superionic-onset and grain-boundary premelting behavior above ~0.9 T m ( T m : melting temperature). These effects are significant in (Fe x Mg 1-x )O (x > 0.8) under core-mantle boundary (CMB) conditions, causing elastic softening, enhanced elemental transport, and ultra-low viscosity. Enhanced diffusion may facilitate core-mantle reactions and the accumulation of Fe-rich material near the CMB, potentially contributing to a dense basal assemblage. Under mantle flow and/or thermal buoyancy, the low viscosity of connected Fe-rich (Fe,Mg)O could favor deformation and redistribution toward shallower depths. This process may contribute to the formation and evolution of some ultra-low velocity zones (ULVZs). The proposed scenario is consistent with the layered structures and inferred low viscosity of some ULVZs and suggests a potential role for Fe-rich (Fe,Mg)O in core-mantle material exchange and heat transfer.

candidates.abstract: Abstract Deep eutectic systems (DESs) are emerging as highly versatile functional materials for 3D printing, particularly in multiphoton 3D laser printing (MPLP), a powerful technique for the fabrication of complex microstructures with high spatial resolution. Here, we present a versatile strategy for the fabrication of multi-state pH-responsive microactuators based on polymerizable DESs using MPLP. By incorporating vinyl phosphonic acid and vinyl imidazole as functional monomers, respectively, we establish two actively responsive DESs that exhibit antagonistic swelling behavior across the pH range while maintaining excellent printability. The printed 3D microstructures show pronounced and reversible pH-responsive actuation with high cycling stability. Combining both materials within single architectures enables multi-state and bidirectional actuation beyond conventional bilayer systems. Complex actuator geometries further demonstrate the versatility of the platform. A hyperelastic theory implemented in a finite element framework can predict the experimentally observed actuation patterns. These results highlight the potential of polymerizable DESs as a new material platform for advanced microscale soft robotic, sensing, and adaptive systems.

candidates.authors: Alexander Klein, Jan Blahut, Suresh K. Vasa, Dmitrii Blokhin, Sven G. Hyberts, Zdeněk Tošner, Rasmus Linser
candidates.abstract: Abstract TROP it or drop it: Owing to fast magic-angle spinning at frequencies above 50 kHz, solid-state nuclear magnetic resonance has evolved as a versatile method to decipher protein structure, dynamics, and chemical properties. While conceptually, higher-dimensional approaches such as 4D and 5D correlation spectra are capable of exceeding the established molecular-weight limitations by ameliorating signal overlap, their intrinsic implications for sensitivity and measurement times required have severely limited these important prospects in practice. Here we show that in high-dimensional experiments, the extensive use of dedicated transverse-mixing optimal control pulses (TROPs) can reduce the necessary measurement time by almost an order of magnitude. TROP’ed non-uniformly sampled experiments not only benefit from a multiplicative sensitivity enhancement in each complex time point due to concomitant transfer of both components of complex signals along multi-step magnetization transfer pathways, but additionally from facilitation of reconstruction with better raw data. Aided by the processing framework provided to future users here, the combination of an extensive use of TROPs with increased dimensionality hence presents itself as highly promising to ameliorate the conventional limitations of solid-state NMR.

candidates.authors: Jung Han Shin, Verner P. Bingman, Sang Ah Lee
candidates.abstract: Episodic memory is grounded upon a spatiotemporal framework that binds discrete event details into a coherent structure. However, the neural mechanisms that construct this scaffold and their potential for memory enhancement through cognitive training have yet to be investigated. Here, we show a common spatiotemporal basis for human episodic memory across distinct populations, using a task in which participants remembered a sequence of objects placed in different locations in a virtual environment. Ultra-high-resolution 7-Tesla fMRI revealed that, within the hippocampal formation, the subiculum exhibited selective responses to spatiotemporal binding across sequences of spatial locations, which we attributed to its compressed, high-dimensional neural representational capacity compared to other hippocampal subfields. We then targeted this spatiotemporal framework through a two-week multi-target navigation training paradigm in a subset of participants, which led to transferable improvements in episodic memory. Critically, these behavioral gains were accompanied by enhanced retrieval-related activation and neural pattern reinstatement in the subiculum, measured using 3-Tesla fMRI. Together, these findings establish the subiculum as a core neural substrate for spatiotemporal scaffolding in human episodic memory and highlight its potential as a target for cognitive interventions. Episodic memories are bound to their spatiotemporal context. High-resolution fMRI revealed that the subiculum, the hippocampus’s main output region, is central to spatiotemporal memory recall and functionally enhanced by navigation training.

candidates.title: Dual-functional-unit modulation enables superior energy storage in high-entropy relaxor ferroelectrics
candidates.authors: Guanfu Liu, Jiyu Wang, Bao Ou, Xiqi Chen, Xuanyu Chen, Yi Cheng, Ran Gao, Bin Li, He Qi, Yejing Dai
candidates.abstract: High-performance dielectric capacitors are indispensable for next-generation pulsed power systems. However, simultaneously achieving high recoverable energy density and efficiency remains challenging because of the intrinsic trade-off between polarization and breakdown strength. Here, we develop a dual-functional-unit modulation strategy to overcome this limitation in Bi0.47Na0.47Ba0.06TiO3-based ceramics through configurational-entropy engineering combined with microstructural optimization. Specifically, configurational entropy simultaneously tailors two key local functional units, namely local polarization configurations and oxygen octahedral tilt configurations. Multicomponent substitution at the A site (Ba2+) and B site (Zn2+/Nb5+) induces fragmented heterogeneous polarization configurations together with weakened and disordered oxygen octahedral tilt, enabling strong field-induced polarization, highly reversible polarization responses, and enhanced intrinsic breakdown strength. Combined with grain refinement and improved densification achieved by high-energy ball milling, which further enhances electrical homogeneity and suppresses interfacial polarization, the optimized ceramic exhibits a breakdown strength of 94 kV mm−1, a large recoverable energy density of 16.19 J cm−3 and a high efficiency of 91.3%. This work establishes dual-functional-unit modulation as an effective design principle for high-entropy relaxor ferroelectrics and provides a general framework for overcoming the polarization-breakdown trade-off in dielectric energy storage materials. Dielectric ceramic capacitors are limited by the polarization–breakdown trade-off. Here, the authors show that high-entropy design overcomes this conflict via local structure regulation and microstructural optimization, achieving 16.19 J cm−3 density and 91.3%.

candidates.authors: Yuchen He, Lu Ling, Garrett Dempsey, Nayiri Kalindjian, Zoie Verghese, Erzhen Chen, Irene Liparulo, Isabel Cho, Vyvylyn Tran, Sanjay Kumar, Andreas Stahl
candidates.abstract: Abstract Beige and white adipocytes reside within the same fat depots but differ in their responses to β-adrenergic stimulation. candidates.abstract: Abstract Anodeless all-solid-state batteries with Ag-C interlayers offer high energy density and long cycle life, yet their operation in cold environments remains limited by poorly understood failure mechanisms. Using operando X-ray absorption spectroscopy, cryogenic-cross-section electron microscopy, and X-ray diffraction, we discover that Li-Ag alloying dynamics are highly temperature-dependent: rapid at 45 °C but kinetically suppressed at 5 °C. At low temperatures, suppressed alloying leads to sluggish lithium transport, internal lithium extrusion, interlayer delamination, and rapid capacity decay. We demonstrate that a brief initial charge at 45 °C permanently activates the interlayer via Li-Ag alloy formation, enabling efficient Li transport even at 5 °C. Full pouch cells following this activation protocol retain 87% of their initial capacity after 250 completed cycles following one formation cycle at 5 °C. After 250 cycles at 5 °C, AAP-treated cells delivered approximately three times the discharge capacity of cells cycled with the fixed-temperature protocol. Such in situ electrochemical alloy activation offers a practical and scalable approach to extend anodeless all-solid-state battery performance to sub-ambient temperatures without material redesign.

candidates.title: Quantum-accurate vibrational and conformational dynamics from small molecules to proteins with machine-learned force fields
candidates.authors: Sergio Suárez-Dou, Miguel Gallegos, Kyunghoon Han, Florian N. Brünig, Joshua T. Berryman, Alexandre Tkatchenko
candidates.abstract: Abstract Biomolecular thermodynamics and spectroscopy depend on relative conformer energies, local curvatures, and collective dipole fluctuations on the potential-energy surface. Conventional molecular mechanics force fields enable large-scale simulations, but their fixed functional forms can misrepresent infrared intensities, mode character, and environment-dependent vibrational response. Here we assess general-purpose machine-learned force fields by using finite-temperature infrared spectra across small molecules, gas-phase peptides, and monomeric, oligomeric, and solvated protein assemblies. To enable this analysis, we introduce QVib, a dataset of 293 molecules and 1366 conformers, together with peptide amide-band benchmarks and p53 oligomerization-domain models, to evaluate vibrational transferability from DFT references to experimental spectra. Across these systems, machine-learned force fields improve over molecular mechanics in reproducing DFT-level forces, vibrational frequencies, densities of states, mode eigenvectors, conformational energetics, and experimental infrared spectra. Among models with explicit long-range electrostatics, SO3LR provides the best accuracy–cost balance of the models tested here. These results show that machine-learned force-field dynamics can recover collective, environment-dependent vibrational landscapes at near-DFT fidelity, enabling spectroscopically validated biomolecular simulations at force-field-like cost.

Current workflows are computationally demanding and require manual intervention, creating bottlenecks for high-throughput applications like structure-based drug discovery. In such contexts, where all protein samples can be assumed to be equivalent at resolutions relevant for image alignment, information about particle poses from previous refinements could be reused. Together with its single-pass operation, these features enable near real-time reconstructions that provide feedback during data acquisition. We demonstrate cryoPARES’s effectiveness through rapid structural determination of seven ligand-bound complexes across four distinct protein targets. We also release three fragment-bound cryo-EM datasets. Cryo-electron microscopy studies often generate multiple datasets of closely related samples. Here, the authors present cryoPARES, a supervised deep-learning framework that reuses prior alignments to rapidly determine particle poses.

candidates.title: Bicontinuous Fibre Formation via Co-precipitate Attenuated Solvent Transfer Induced Assembly
candidates.authors: Shankar P. Kharal, Yawei Gao, Luyu Bo, Joshua T. Damron, Michael D. Toomey, Nihal Kanbargi, Sumit Gupta, Changwoo Do, Christopher C. Bowland, Zhenhua Tian, Michelle K. Kidder, Logan T. Kearney, Amit K. Naskar
candidates.abstract: Abstract Polymer–solvent–nonsolvent mixtures provide a versatile route for fabricating structured materials through liquid–liquid phase separation. In this context, solvent transfer–induced phase separation (STrIPS) enables the continuous formation of bicontinuous fibres, yet the process is often limited by coarsening of pores or collapse within the fibre core, leading to structural inhomogeneity. Here, we advance this strategy through Co-precipitate Attenuated Solvent Transfer induced assembly (CAST), in which amphiphilic species precipitate in situ during solvent exchange and preferentially retained within the polymer rich phase. These precipitates act as a distributed molecular retarding agent that delays domain growth, thereby preserving bicontinuity throughout the fibre cross-section to up to 250 µm. Using a poly (ethylene glycol) diacrylate–ethanol–water system with a phenolic oligomer coprecipitate, we demonstrate that CAST stabilizes the hollow bicontinuous domain structure, extending the attainable specific surface area by ca. 100%. Scattering experiments and molecular dynamics simulations confirm that the precipitating species suppress coarsening by restricting mobility within the phase they occupy. Embedding CAST fibres within polydimethylsiloxane demonstrates lightweight composites with sound mitigation capabilities, highlighting the potential for acoustic applications. CAST thus establishes a versatile route to high-performance porous materials with broad potential for structural, acoustic, and energy applications.

candidates.abstract: Abstract Two-dimensional materials exhibit pronounced layer-dependent properties, making accurate determination of atomic-layer thickness essential. Existing characterization techniques typically rely on spectroscopic signatures or scanning probes, which require complex instrumentation and often lack direct real-space interpretability. Here we introduce a spin-dependent optical differentiation approach that encodes thickness into directly observable edge features. By engineering the optical transfer function at planar interfaces, we access anisotropic and isotropic differentiation regimes governed by the spin Hall effect of light. In the anisotropic regime, the layer number is continuously encoded in the orientation of edge features. In the isotropic regime, a morphology-based transition, from disk to ring, provides a discrete and robust signature for layer identification. We experimentally demonstrate layer-resolved imaging in graphene, MoS 2 , and WSe 2 . Our results establish spin-dependent optical differentiation as a simple and versatile platform for translating atomic-scale variations into directly accessible optical features, enabling rapid and in situ characterization of two-dimensional materials.

candidates.title: Real estate wealth inequality and exposure to natural disasters with evidence from France
candidates.authors: Thomas Bézy
candidates.abstract: Most studies measuring inequalities in exposure to climate disasters rely on aggregate income data and focus on residents. By omitting dwellings owned by nonresidents, this approach overlooks half of the housing stock exposed to flooding. Using dwelling-level data covering the entire French housing market, this paper examines how natural disaster risks are distributed across tenants, owner-occupants, and owners of rental, second, and vacant properties. The results highlight large differences with the standard approach that focuses on residents. Once properties owned by nonresidents are included, flood risk disproportionately affects second homes, while subsidence mainly affects owner-occupied dwellings. These patterns have important policy implications. First, untargeted flood insurance subsidies tend to benefit second homes, whereas subsidence coverage mainly supports owner-occupied dwellings. Second, this study shows that natural disaster risks are not priced into rental, second, and vacant properties, driving at least 15% of the total overvaluation in flood-prone areas. Most studies on climate disaster exposure exclude nonresidents, missing about half of housing in floodplains. Including them in France reveals major differences, with implications for subsidized insurance and housing overvaluation.

This shift yields a discharge capacity of ~60,000 mAh g −1 . Beyond its role as a positive electrode catalyst, this architecture functions as a multifunctional interfacial protective layer that stabilizes the lithium metal negative electrode by suppressing dendrite growth. Consequently, the lithium–oxygen system achieves stable lifespan of 2075 cycles under the four-electron pathway with reduced voltage decay. This work establishes a data-guided strategy for the rational design of atomic-scale architecture via artificial intelligence, unlocking the potential of multi-electron oxygen chemistry for lithium–oxygen batteries.

candidates.authors: Shouvik Sur, Lei Chen, Yiming Wang, Chandan Setty, Silke Paschen, Qimiao Si
candidates.abstract: In topological materials, Berry curvature leads to intrinsic Hall responses. Motivated by recent developments in Weyl-Kondo semimetals, here we advance a fully nonequilibrium (FNE) Hall response due to the Berry curvature. In particular, we show that, while the spontaneous Hall current is quadratic in the previously described regime of weak electric field, due to the contribution from the dipole moment of the Berry curvature, the FNE Hall response for non-perturbative electric fields is not controlled by the Berry curvature dipole. We illustrate the universality of these results by comparing them with their counterparts in systems with any higher-multipole of the Berry curvature. candidates.abstract: In a strongly interacting Rydberg atom array, the dynamics are often constrained to the decoupled Hilbert subspaces, representing an intriguing paradigm for nonergodicity. By considering a variable detuning of the global Rydberg coupling, we show that, not only is the existence of these Hilbert subspaces dependent on the interplay of detuning and interaction, but they are also strongly fragmented, with the fragment dimensions exhibiting various scaling behaviors with increasing system size. The resulting constrained dynamics of the system are thus governed by the dimension and connectivity of these fragments. We then adopt an auxiliary fermion description to reveal the underlying emergent kinetic constraints for the subspace fragmentation and fragment-confined dynamics. candidates.title: Fluctuation-Response Theory of Nonequilibrium Complex Fluids
candidates.authors: Ryota Takaki, Frank Jülicher
candidates.abstract: A fundamental challenge in soft matter physics is to describe materials, such as the living cytoplasm and tissues, that are simultaneously active, chemically driven, and exhibit long-lasting memory of mechanical stresses. Here, we construct a generalized hydrodynamic framework at finite wave vectors and frequencies that is applicable to nonequilibrium fluids with memory. By leveraging stationary correlation identities, we derive a generalized linear response theory for nonequilibrium steady states. This framework serves as a formal extension of Onsager’s regression hypothesis beyond thermal equilibrium. Our approach provides a direct pathway to derive transport coefficients from steady-state fluctuations without the traditional Mori-Zwanzig projection-operator formalism, generalizing the Green-Kubo relations to nonequilibrium systems. As a corollary, we derive two model-free variants of the nonequilibrium fluctuation-response relation for non-Markovian dynamics. These generalized relations explicitly capture the nonequilibrium circulating currents—an out-of-equilibrium signature that is invisible to conventional scalar formulations or frameworks that treat degrees of freedom independently. Applying our theory to chemically driven active fluids reveals the emergence of active viscoelastic memory, wherein chemical reaction cycles dynamically renormalize the macroscopic viscous response. Strikingly, this active memory can induce negative storage modulus at finite frequencies, a behavior absent in ordinary viscoelastic fluids. Our first-principles framework rigorously extends linear rheology to nonequilibrium systems and provides a foundation for understanding non-Markovian dynamics across a broad range of biological and synthetic active matter.

candidates.abstract: Topological properties of microscopic configurations may provide additional insight into phase transitions beyond conventional thermodynamic observables. We investigate this idea in the two-dimensional Ising model on square and triangular lattices by associating cell complexes with the positive and negative spin domains and constructing an Euler-characteristic observable from their difference. We provide the expression relating this quantity to conventional observables of the Ising model. This derivation allows us to understand its expected behavior physically. As a byproduct, we show that at any finite positive temperature the expectation of the Euler characteristic exceeds a positive, lattice-size-independent bound, hence disproving a previously suggested conjecture. Monte Carlo simulations combined with multihistogram reweighting show that this spin-odd topological observable exhibits order-parameter-like behavior near the ferromagnetic transition. Finite-size scaling of its susceptibility yields pseudocritical temperatures that converge to the known critical temperature for both lattice geometries. On the square lattice, the leading-order estimate of the critical exponent obtained from the topological observable depends more strongly on the fitting range than the magnetization estimate. This behavior is consistent with stronger subleading finite-size corrections, as supported by fits including an additional correction term. On the triangular lattice, the corresponding estimate remains consistent with the theoretical Ising value. Our study suggests that topologically defined quantities such as the Euler characteristic can provide an alternative way to locate order-disorder phase transitions in the systems considered here. Since the definition of these observables is purely geometrical, they can provide useful insights in cases in which order parameters cannot be constructed.

The most widely used, Tammann's rule, places reaction onset at two-thirds of the lowest precursor melting point, but has never been systematically tested. Using an automated laboratory, we heated 1,035 pairwise combinations of 46 common precursors at their Tammann temperatures and identified the products by x-ray diffraction. Only 25% of pairs formed products containing both precursors. Combining these outcomes with text-mined literature syntheses, we trained log-normal accelerated failure time models that treat each fixed-temperature experiment as a bound on the unknown onset temperature. On 26 reactions with onset temperatures measured by in situ x-ray diffraction, a three-descriptor model reduced the mean absolute error from 131°C (Tammann's rule) to 88°C; adding 29 further physicochemical descriptors did not improve the model. Reaction onset can therefore be predicted from routine pass/fail synthesis outcomes, and predictions will improve as such data accumulates.

candidates.abstract: Coherent control of fermions has become a standard approach for engineering quantum devices. Here, we explore parity-induced frustration in multiterminal Josephson arrays. We focus on odd-parity Josephson trijunctions, where the presence of a trapped fermion induces a phase winding in each trijunction. Connecting these trijunctions constrains their shared phases, resulting in a long-distance phase coherence where the frustrated configurations dominate the low-energy physics. In the classical regime, these arrays map onto the Kagome XY antiferromagnet, whose established Berezinskii-Kosterlitz-Thouless (BKT) transition yields algebraically decaying $6e$ phase correlations. We show that the $6e$ phase coherence is manifested as a pronounced third harmonic in the current-phase relation of these arrays. While quantum phase fluctuations suppress the $6e$ coherence, we show that through spin-orbit coupling they also lead to spin correlations and entanglement between the trapped fermions. candidates.abstract: Understanding the minimal model that captures the essential physics of infinite-layer nickelate superconductors remains a central challenge. Using first-principles density-functional theory combined with dynamical mean-field theory (DFT+DMFT), we compute and compare the strongly correlated electronic structures and optical spectra of various effective models for the infinite-layer nickelate LaNiO$_2$, ranging from a $d_{x^2-y^2}$ 1-band model to a full 6-band model with all Ni-$3d$ plus an interstitial-$s$ orbital. The results demonstrate that Ni-$3d$ 5-band models overestimate the Hundness picture, whereas 6-band models, which explicitly include the interstitial-$s$ band and have an $A$-pocket, recover the characteristic Mottness physics. Importantly, the influence of the interstitial-$s$ band on the correlations of the $d_{x^2-y^2}$ band is negligible. Thus, superconductivity in infinite-layer nickelates can be reliably described within a single-band Hubbard framework, while the accurate description of inter-orbital properties such as (optical) conductivities requires the inclusion of at least the interstitial-$s$ band.
